title: Endosymbiosis: Did Complex Life Begin with a Merger?
question: How did the complex cells of animals, plants and fungi arise, and why did it apparently happen only once?
summary: Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria swallowed by another cell. This single partnership may have unlocked the energy budget that complex life required.
content:
Two Kinds of Cell

Life on Earth divides into prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea), which are small and structurally simple, and eukaryotes, whose cells contain a nucleus, internal compartments and mitochondria. For roughly two billion years prokaryotes were the only life. Eukaryotes then appeared, and every animal, plant, fungus and alga descends from that lineage. There are almost no intermediate forms. The jump looks abrupt.

Lynn Margulis's Heresy

In 1967 Lynn Margulis argued that mitochondria and chloroplasts were once independent bacteria that took up residence inside another cell. The idea was ridiculed for years, but the evidence accumulated. Mitochondria have their own circular DNA, divide on their own like bacteria, are wrapped in a double membrane, and their genes are most closely related to those of alpha-proteobacteria. Chloroplasts trace to cyanobacteria. Genome sequencing later placed the host cell among the archaea, specifically the Asgard group.

The Energy Argument

Nick Lane and Bill Martin argued in 2010 that the merger was not incidental but necessary. A bacterium makes ATP across its outer membrane, so as it grows its energy supply scales with surface area while its needs scale with volume. Bacteria therefore cannot grow genomes much larger without becoming inefficient. Mitochondria moved energy production inside the cell, with hundreds or thousands of small, specialized membranes per cell. Per gene, a eukaryote can then spend on the order of thousands of times more energy than a bacterium, paying for large genomes, elaborate regulation and eventually multicellularity.

Why Only Once?

Bacteria and archaea have had billions of years to repeat the trick, yet the eukaryotic lineage appears to have a single origin. One explanation is that the event is intrinsically improbable: a host must survive engulfing a bacterium, avoid being killed, and reach a stable symbiosis where genes migrate to the nucleus. Another is that once eukaryotes existed, they filled the niche and excluded newcomers. We have a sample size of one, which makes either explanation hard to test.

Implications

If complex life depended on a rare event, then microbial life might be common in the universe while animals, plants and minds are rare. That makes endosymbiosis relevant to the Fermi paradox as well as to biology.

perspectives.title: The Cell Biologist
perspectives.description: Genomic and structural evidence shows that mitochondria and plastids are domesticated bacteria. The nucleus, the membrane systems and the cytoskeleton still have debated origins.

perspectives.title: The Bioenergetics View
perspectives.description: Complex life is limited by energy per gene. Internalizing respiration let genome size and cell complexity escape the constraints that cap bacteria.

perspectives.title: The Evolutionary Theorist
perspectives.description: Symbiosis shows that evolution is not only gradual branching. Lineages can fuse and produce a new individual, which stretches the picture of a strictly tree-shaped history.

perspectives.title: The Astrobiologist
perspectives.description: If the merger was a freak accident, the universe may hold abundant microbes and very few complex ecosystems. If it was nearly inevitable, complex life should be common.

openQuestions: What was the host cell like, and did it already have a nucleus before acquiring mitochondria?
Was the partnership driven by metabolism, protection or something else?
Why do no modern prokaryotes show a partial path to this complexity?
Could a different route to complexity exist, using a mechanism other than endosymbiosis?
How would we recognize complex life elsewhere if its history differs?
